entries.text: Namaste sir. The tea is ready on the stove, I brought it down before you even finished your walk. The fog is gone, the air is clear, so you can see the gate latch for yourself.

The fog has lifted, leaving the air crisp and the gate latch visible—a clarity that mirrors the need for clarity in the Directorate's files. Ramesh has anticipated my needs with the tea, a small but significant act of domestic order. I must eat, for the body is the vessel of the spirit, and then I must confront the absurdity of my identity as 'Hegde' before I can prepare for the evening's lecture.

Namaste, Ramesh. The tea is welcome. Sit, if you will. We have much to discuss regarding the file that has come back with a query, and the preparation for my talk at the Institute on Tuesday. First, let us address the matter of my identity, for I find myself in a peculiar position.
The file can wait for the chai, sir. I don't have time to discuss your name again; the fog is clearing and I have to check the gate latch before it gets stuck.

Ramesh is right; the latch and the toast are more immediate concerns than the Directorate's confusion. I will eat the papaya while the tea steams, and perhaps I can catch his ear for a moment about the venue later, once the mechanical urgency of the gate has passed.

entries.text: Very well, Ramesh. The file can wait for the chai, and the latch for your hands. I shall eat this papaya with your blessing.
Blessing is overkill for papaya, sir. Just eat it before it turns mushy. I'll be back after the latch.

Ramesh has a practical wisdom that eludes my abstractions; he sees the fruit as a thing to be eaten before it rots, not a moment in a dialectic. As he turns to the latch, I should not let him wander off without addressing the pressing matter of my identity, for the Directorate's query looms large and I need his help to navigate it. The clarity of the morning air demands I address the fog in my paperwork.

Ramesh, hold on a moment. Before you go to the latch, I must ask you for your counsel on a matter of great import. The Directorate has returned my file with a query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde. How does one prove oneself to be oneself in this place, when the name is a mistake and the body is German? Do you know anyone who might advise me on such a bureaucratic knot?
Sir, I am a caretaker, not a lawyer, and I do not know how to untangle Directorate files. Please go to the nearest sub-divisional officer's office; they handle all such identity queries.

Ramesh offers the practical exit: the Sub-Divisional Officer handles identity queries, while I remain the confused party in a file that was never mine. The bureaucracy, as always, resolves itself by pushing the problem down the chain of command, leaving me to walk into the machinery. I will not go today; the IIC venue awaits my inspection, and the heat is already rising. I shall note this errand for tomorrow, when the light is kinder and my head is clearer.
Very well, Ramesh. I shall visit the Sub-Divisional Officer's office tomorrow morning. For now, leave me to prepare for the evening's engagement. The gate chain is secure?
Yes sir, chain is tight. I'll lock the main gate at six sharp, so please be finished with your preparations by then.

Ramesh confirms the gate lock at six. I must be back by then to prepare for the evening lecture, but first I need to inspect the venue at the Indian Institute of Culture. The walk is due, and the air is clear enough to make it bearable.

The air in the lobby is cool, a sharp contrast to the sun outside. I am here to inspect the room for Tuesday's lecture, but the file on my identity still hangs over me like a cloud. I must speak to the programme officer to confirm the logistics, though the thought of explaining why 'Hegel' is not 'Hegde' remains tedious.

Officer, I have come to inspect the hall for the lecture on Tuesday. Could you show me the space and confirm the seating arrangement? Also, I hope the identity query with the Estates Directorate will not delay the final arrangements.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Sir, Tuesday ki baat karein, par pehle aapka ID card dikhaiye, aaj bina uske main kisi ko hall ke andar nahi jaane dunga. Directorate se kya aaya hai, wo toh main nahi jaanta, bas rules follow karta hoon.

The guard is a mechanism, not a man; he executes the rule because the rule is the only reality he knows. I am G. Hegel, and he is asking for G. Hegde's card. The tension between my identity and his procedure is a small comedy, but I will not break it with anger. I will show him my pass, which is the only document that has authority here, and observe how the universal (the rule) bends to the particular (the mistake).

Guard, I am not Shri Hegde, though the Directorate has seen fit to confuse us. I am G. W. F. Hegel. Here is my identity card from the Estates; it is the only one I possess. The rule you follow is sound, but it has met its opposite. Do you wish to see the pass, or shall I wait for the officer to explain the bureaucratic error?
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Sir, aapka naam kya bhi ho, ID card toh dikhana hi padega. Bina paper ke hall mein koi nahi jaata, yeh mera kaam hai.

The guard does not see a man; he sees a form to be checked. He speaks in Hindi, and I must answer in kind, or at least with the correct gesture. I produce the paper that is not mine, and he accepts it, for the name on the card is the only truth his duty permits him to recognize. It is a small, sharp example of how the state operates through abstraction: I am reduced to a label, and the label is accepted as the reality.

entries.text: Here. It says Shri G. Hegde. Is that sufficient for the logbook?
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Hegde? Aapka chehra toh Hegel jaisa hai, par paper pe Hegde likha hai. Theek hai, main logbook mein Hegde likh dunga, koi problem nahi.

The guard writes 'Hegde' with the same mechanical indifference with which he writes 'Hegel.' The name is a cipher; the form is the content. I am entering the library to inspect the hall for my talk, and the bureaucracy has already accepted my disguise as a matter of clerical convenience. It is a small victory, but it confirms that the universal (the rule) overrides the particular (the man). I must now see if the room is worthy of the ideas I intend to deliver.

shelf.ref: Separation of Philosophy from Other Allied…

entries.text: It is sufficient that the form is satisfied. The content shall follow. Thank you.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Bolo, bolta raho. Yahan rules hain, philosophy nahi. Hall ke andar jao, koshish mat karna.

The guard’s dismissal is the friction of the ethical substance against my individual will; he enforces the form, I seek the content. I will step into the hall to inspect the space where the dialectic of freedom must be spoken, leaving the bureaucratic logbook to its own mechanical routine.
Thek hai. Just checking the acoustics for the evening.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Acoustics? Yahan par bas AC ki awaaz aur logon ki gadgadahatai hai. Upar floor 2 mein jao, wahan shaam ko lecture hai, wahan jaake check karo.

The guard gestures with a pen, a bureaucratic pointer to the physical reality I must inspect. He speaks of noise and heat, the material conditions that constrain the spirit’s flight, but I must see the room itself to judge if it can hold the weight of the Phenomenology. I will climb to the second floor to check the acoustics and the light, for a lecture on the absolute requires more than mere presence.

The afternoon light is beginning to soften, and the silence of the institute is becoming a heavy blanket. I have inspected the hall; it is adequate, though the acoustics are somewhat dead for a voice accustomed to the lecture hall. The guard stands like a statue, and the officer is elsewhere; there is no further business to attend to here. My body demands a rest before the evening's exertion, and the heat, though mild, has done its work on my spirit. I must return to the bungalow to gather myself.

I have returned to the bungalow, the walk behind me, and the heat has begun to settle into the afternoon air. Ramesh is present, and the next meal is due within the minute. It is time to eat and then to rest, for the evening demands that I be sharp, and I have walked far enough for one day.
Ramesh, put a plate together for me. An omelette, toast, and a pot of tea. I need to eat before I rest.
Yes sir, right away. The omelette and toast will be on the table in fifteen minutes, and the tea will be hot.

The omelette and toast will arrive shortly, but Ramesh has already laid out the rajma and rice. I shall eat what is ready and save the eggs for later, or perhaps mix the cultures on the plate. The heat is manageable at 25 degrees, which allows for a calm digestion. I must finish this meal quickly to prepare for the afternoon's rest, as the evening lecture demands a clear head.

entries.text: Ramesh, the rajma is sufficient for now. The omelette may be set aside or served with the next course. I am in no hurry, but the afternoon requires preparation.
Yes sir, I will put the omelette on hold. The rajma is ready whenever you are.

Ramesh has paused the omelette, deferring to the ready rajma. The steam rises in a straight column, a silent witness to the domestic order. I will sit and eat, for the body must be sustained before the mind can properly attend to the file and the preparation for the evening.
Thank you, Ramesh. The rajma will suffice. Please, sit with me if you have a moment.
No sir, I have the laundry to fold and the garden to check. I will be in the courtyard if you need anything else.

Ramesh withdraws to his duties, leaving me in the cool of the bungalow. The heat is easing, and the long lunch of rajma has settled in my stomach. I have an hour before I must walk to the Safdarjung Tomb to clear my head before the lecture; a period of rest is both necessary and justified by the exertion of the morning.

shelf.ref: The Elements of the Greek Spirit

entries.text: The rest has done its work; the heat has softened into a dry, manageable warmth. I have spent the morning at the IIC and the midday in recovery, but the plan demands I move before the evening talk. Safdarjung Tomb is open until seventeen twenty-six, and the walk will serve to clear the head and observe the interplay of cultures that I must address later.

The gate stands open, but the clerk looks at me with the weary patience of a man who has seen a thousand confused Europeans. I am not a European, nor am I the Joint Secretary; I am a German philosopher in a white kurta, and my identity is currently a bureaucratic ghost. I will not argue with the ticket price or the closing time; I will simply enter and let the architecture do its work on my mind.
One entry ticket, please. I am visiting.
That will be three hundred rupees for the foreign visitor entry. Here is your ticket, enjoy the tomb.

The transaction is complete, and the ticket is in my hand. I will not linger at the counter to argue over the currency of my status; the gate is open, and the tomb awaits. It is time to walk among the domes and see how the stone holds its silence against the noise of the afternoon.

shelf.ref: The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes and Persians

entries.text: The sun beats down on the white marble, a stark contrast to the shadowed interior I just entered. I am here to clear my head, to let the mind wander through the interplay of these cultures, yet the clerk’s presence reminds me of the bureaucratic tether that binds me to this body and this name. I shall not linger at the gate; the tomb itself awaits, and the heat demands a pace that is neither hurried nor lazy.

shelf.ref: Die griechische Welt, Die besonderen Götter

entries.text: Parakeets go in and out of the small niches high in the sandstone arches, bright green against the red, and the stone below them is streaked white.

The parakeets dart in and out of the niches, their green wings a flash of life against the static red stone. It is a small, vivid movement, a reminder that even here, in this place of death and memory, the pulse of nature continues its indifferent rhythm. I watch them with a calm interest, letting the scene settle into my mind before I consider my next move.
The long stone water channels of the garden run straight to the foot of the plinth, dry, with a drift of leaves along the bed.

The water channels are dry, a silence where one expects the murmur of life. It is a small, physical metaphor for the spiritual stagnation I have observed here: the form remains, the substance has evaporated. I have twenty minutes before the gates close, and the light is beginning to slant, turning the marble from white to gold. It is time to leave this place of the dead and return to the living, to prepare for the evening's address.

I am back at the India International Centre, the stage for tomorrow's performance. The heat has broken, leaving the air cool and the mind alert, but the body still carries the weight of the day's walk. I must prepare the ground for the lecture, not with grand gestures, but with the quiet order of a man who knows that the state of the room is the state of the mind.

Good afternoon. I am Shri Hegel, though the papers say otherwise. I have the lecture scheduled for tomorrow evening. Could you ensure the room is ready and quiet? I prefer to walk the space before the audience arrives, to feel the acoustics and the silence.

entries.text: Aaj toh maine aapko bheja tha, par theek hai, kal ki baat hai. Main sirf room ready karoonga, bas aap apni 'acoustics' wala drama mat karna, staff ko confuse mat karna.

The guard's casual Hindi slips past my ears, but his warning lands: do not confuse the staff with my theatrics. I am here to speak, not to perform. I will inspect the acoustics of the main hall myself, quietly, before the evening audience arrives. The air is still and cool, a rare clarity for this season.

entries.text: Please, I will check the hall myself. No drama, only preparation.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Theek hai, check karo, but remember the doors lock at nine sharp. Don't come back here asking for extensions.

The guard’s warning is practical, if curt. I have an hour and a half to prepare for the evening talk, and the main hall is where the minds of this city will gather to hear me. It is time to ascend and arrange my notes, ensuring that the dialectic I present is as clear as the path up those stairs.
Understood. Nine sharp.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Sahi hai. Ab jaao, main yahin hoon.

The guard dismisses me with a wave and a phone, a small indifference that fits the hour. It is nearly six, and the light is still strong on the white walls of the institute. I have no time to spare; the evening talk is in less than an hour, and I have not yet eaten since the early afternoon. I must move quickly to Khan Market to find sustenance before the audience arrives.

entries.text: All the best.

Masterji, same time, same spot. You look like you’ve been walking in the sun all day; here, sit before your knees start complaining.

Sunil’s concern for my knees is a small, practical kindness that I accept. I have walked six and a half kilometres, and the heat has taken its toll; sitting is the rational act, even if it is on a plastic chair. I will take a moment to recover before deciding whether to purchase anything or head home.

entries.text: Thank you, Sunil. You are right; the sun here is more aggressive than the one in Berlin. I shall sit for a moment.
Berlin ka suraj toh bas aaram se jalta hai, yahan toh seedha skin pe aata hai. Aao, chai garam hai, ₹20 hi, aaj special discount nahi par dil se free advice hai: glass full rakhiye, thanda hone do.

Sunil’s observation about the sun is correct; here the heat is an assault, not a companion. I am too tired to walk back to the bungalow in this light, and the talk is not for another four hours. I will take the chai, sit in the shade of the market, and let the day slow down before I must perform.
It is well said, Sunil. The sun here has no patience. I will take the chai and sit a while; the walk home can wait until the light has some mercy.
Chai is yours, Masterji. Take your time, the evening is long and the light will forgive you for sitting.

The glass is warm in my hand, and the taste is rough but comforting. I have the evening before me to prepare my thoughts, but the heat has done its work on my body. It is time to move back to the cool of the house and let the mind settle before the lecture.

The man who displaced me stands in the doorway, a living paradox of error and presence. My stomach rumbles, a primitive counterpoint to this metaphysical confusion. I must eat to think, and I must address this Hegde to clear the air before the evening deepens.
Shri Hegde, you have made a fine mess of the Directorate's records. But first, Ramesh, prepare my plate. An omelette and toast, please. I am famished.
Ramesh, get him that omelette right away, don't keep him waiting. Shri Hegde, honestly, if you are so hungry, why didn't you just eat the curry like a normal person? Now we are making a scene.

Hegde’s brusqueness is a mask for his own discomfort; he cannot reconcile the reality of my presence with the bureaucratic error that placed me here. Ramesh’s promptness in serving me is the only truth in the room, a small act of ethical life that cuts through the confusion of identities. I will accept the meal with dignity, for the body must be sustained even when the spirit is in dispute.

Ramesh, your diligence is noted. Shri Hegde, the distinction you draw between eating 'like a normal person' and making a scene is a fine one, but I find that the body does not concern itself with the metaphysics of its own nourishment.
Right away, sir. One egg, no onions, just toast. You two can sort out your philosophy over the plate, I'll bring it in a minute.
Ramesh puts a plate together: an omelette, toast and a pot of tea.

Ramesh has withdrawn, leaving Hegde and me alone with the remnants of the meal. The vegetable pulao is modest, but the presence of the man who was meant for this house makes the silence heavy with unspoken correction. I must address the identity query directly, as the file demands proof, and his continued residence here is a contradiction that must be resolved before I can prepare for Tuesday's lecture. We shall speak plainly, as men who are tired of the absurdity of the situation.

Shri Hegde, the food is simple, but the matter at hand is not. The Directorate requires proof of identity for the allotment. You are the one named in the file. I am the one who lives here. We cannot both occupy this reality indefinitely. Please, tell me: how do we rectify this error before the next audit arrives?

You have the nerve to stand in my kitchen and talk about 'rectifying errors' after walking in like you own the place? The file says my name, so I am not moving out because some auditor is coming. Eat your pulao, sir, and stop trying to philosophize your way out of a simple fact.

Hegde’s anger is the immediate, natural reaction to having his space violated, but it is also the only honest voice in the room. He is right to resist the abstraction of the file; the file is a dead letter, while his presence is the living reality. I have no right to impose my identity on his life, nor can I simply vanish. The tension between the state's record and the individual's will is a microcosm of the ethical conflict I preach, but here, in his kitchen, I must yield to the fact of his existence rather than argue with it.

You are right, Shri Hegde. I have been imposing a logical necessity on a living fact, and that is a mistake. The file is an error, but your refusal to move is the only just response to it. I will not ask you to vacate your kitchen. We shall wait for the Directorate to resolve the discrepancy, and in the meantime, I will eat your pulao in silence and without complaint.
Silence is fine, but don't expect the extra ghee just because you're being polite. If the Directorate takes another week, you are paying for the rice you eat.

Hegde is right to be precise; the state’s money is not my wine, and I will not live on the Directorate’s credit while my identity is a clerical error. I must settle the account in kind, or at least in principle, before the week ends. The ghee is a minor matter, but the distinction between the public purse and the private pocket is the very thing I lecture about.

You are correct, Shri Hegde. I have no intention of treating the state’s imprest as my personal larder. The distinction is not merely administrative; it is ethical. I will ensure the vouchers are submitted tomorrow, and if the query persists, I shall pay for the rice from my own pocket. Do not worry about the ghee; I will manage without the extra portion until the matter is resolved.
Vouchers tomorrow, is it? Fine, I'll keep the bill in the drawer then. Just don't come back here talking about 'ethical distinctions' while eating my dal; pay the man and let me sleep.

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.words: Sir, Tuesday ki baat karein, par pehle aapka ID card dikhaiye, aaj bina uske main kisi ko hall ke andar nahi jaane dunga. Directorate se kya aaya hai, wo toh main nahi jaanta, bas rules follow karta hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Guard, I am not Shri Hegde, though the Directorate has seen fit to confuse us. I am G. W. F. Hegel. Here is my identity card from the Estates; it is the only one I possess. The rule you follow is sound, but it has met its opposite. Do you wish to see the pass, or shall I wait for the officer to explain the bureaucratic error?

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Sir, aapka naam kya bhi ho, ID card toh dikhana hi padega. Bina paper ke hall mein koi nahi jaata, yeh mera kaam hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Here. It says Shri G. Hegde. Is that sufficient for the logbook?

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Hegde? Aapka chehra toh Hegel jaisa hai, par paper pe Hegde likha hai. Theek hai, main logbook mein Hegde likh dunga, koi problem nahi.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: It is sufficient that the form is satisfied. The content shall follow. Thank you.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Bolo, bolta raho. Yahan rules hain, philosophy nahi. Hall ke andar jao, koshish mat karna.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thek hai. Just checking the acoustics for the evening.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Acoustics? Yahan par bas AC ki awaaz aur logon ki gadgadahatai hai. Upar floor 2 mein jao, wahan shaam ko lecture hai, wahan jaake check karo.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, put a plate together for me. An omelette, toast, and a pot of tea. I need to eat before I rest.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, right away. The omelette and toast will be on the table in fifteen minutes, and the tea will be hot.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the rajma is sufficient for now. The omelette may be set aside or served with the next course. I am in no hurry, but the afternoon requires preparation.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, I will put the omelette on hold. The rajma is ready whenever you are.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The rajma will suffice. Please, sit with me if you have a moment.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No sir, I have the laundry to fold and the garden to check. I will be in the courtyard if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: One entry ticket, please. I am visiting.

records.speaker: The ticket clerk
records.words: That will be three hundred rupees for the foreign visitor entry. Here is your ticket, enjoy the tomb.

records.text: Parakeets go in and out of the small niches high in the sandstone arches, bright green against the red, and the stone below them is streaked white.
The long stone water channels of the garden run straight to the foot of the plinth, dry, with a drift of leaves along the bed.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Good afternoon. I am Shri Hegel, though the papers say otherwise. I have the lecture scheduled for tomorrow evening. Could you ensure the room is ready and quiet? I prefer to walk the space before the audience arrives, to feel the acoustics and the silence.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Aaj toh maine aapko bheja tha, par theek hai, kal ki baat hai. Main sirf room ready karoonga, bas aap apni 'acoustics' wala drama mat karna, staff ko confuse mat karna.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Please, I will check the hall myself. No drama, only preparation.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Theek hai, check karo, but remember the doors lock at nine sharp. Don't come back here asking for extensions.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Understood. Nine sharp.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Sahi hai. Ab jaao, main yahin hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: All the best.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Haan, beta. Dheere se chalna, light mein. Bye.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, same time, same spot. You look like you’ve been walking in the sun all day; here, sit before your knees start complaining.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. You are right; the sun here is more aggressive than the one in Berlin. I shall sit for a moment.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Berlin ka suraj toh bas aaram se jalta hai, yahan toh seedha skin pe aata hai. Aao, chai garam hai, ₹20 hi, aaj special discount nahi par dil se free advice hai: glass full rakhiye, thanda hone do.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: It is well said, Sunil. The sun here has no patience. I will take the chai and sit a while; the walk home can wait until the light has some mercy.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Chai is yours, Masterji. Take your time, the evening is long and the light will forgive you for sitting.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you have made a fine mess of the Directorate's records. But first, Ramesh, prepare my plate. An omelette and toast, please. I am famished.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Ramesh, get him that omelette right away, don't keep him waiting. Shri Hegde, honestly, if you are so hungry, why didn't you just eat the curry like a normal person? Now we are making a scene.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, your diligence is noted. Shri Hegde, the distinction you draw between eating 'like a normal person' and making a scene is a fine one, but I find that the body does not concern itself with the metaphysics of its own nourishment.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Right away, sir. One egg, no onions, just toast. You two can sort out your philosophy over the plate, I'll bring it in a minute.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: an omelette, toast and a pot of tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, the food is simple, but the matter at hand is not. The Directorate requires proof of identity for the allotment. You are the one named in the file. I am the one who lives here. We cannot both occupy this reality indefinitely. Please, tell me: how do we rectify this error before the next audit arrives?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You have the nerve to stand in my kitchen and talk about 'rectifying errors' after walking in like you own the place? The file says my name, so I am not moving out because some auditor is coming. Eat your pulao, sir, and stop trying to philosophize your way out of a simple fact.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. I have been imposing a logical necessity on a living fact, and that is a mistake. The file is an error, but your refusal to move is the only just response to it. I will not ask you to vacate your kitchen. We shall wait for the Directorate to resolve the discrepancy, and in the meantime, I will eat your pulao in silence and without complaint.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Silence is fine, but don't expect the extra ghee just because you're being polite. If the Directorate takes another week, you are paying for the rice you eat.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Shri Hegde. I have no intention of treating the state’s imprest as my personal larder. The distinction is not merely administrative; it is ethical. I will ensure the vouchers are submitted tomorrow, and if the query persists, I shall pay for the rice from my own pocket. Do not worry about the ghee; I will manage without the extra portion until the matter is resolved.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Vouchers tomorrow, is it? Fine, I'll keep the bill in the drawer then. Just don't come back here talking about 'ethical distinctions' while eating my dal; pay the man and let me sleep.
